newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone talks agree truce, further dialogue.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone talks agree truce, further dialogue.

text.p: West African foreign ministers and envoys of Sierra Leone's military rulers agreed on Friday that there should be an immediate halt to any fighting throughout the battered nation.

A statement, read by Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi after a second day of talks in Ivory Coast, said that the two sides agreed "to resolve all issues related to the Sierra Leone crisis peacefully".
It said the two sides, trying to defuse a standoff over a May 25 military coup in the capital Freetown, had agreed to adjourn their meeting and meet again next Friday.

Nigerian troops, in Sierra Leone under a pre-coup defence pact, have clashed with junta forces and their rebel allies. So too, have members of a Kamajor traditional hunter militia given extra powers by ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
Junta spokesman Allieu Kamara told reporters the truce deal meant the borders and airport would reopen. "No more blockades. The airport will be open. No more hostilities," he said.
Sierra Leone's neighbours decided in Guinea on June 26 to pursue dialogue and economic sanctions to try to persuade the junta to reinstate Kabbah, but they retained a military option.
The statement said the two sides would "work towards early restoration of constitutional order". It did not elaborate. It said a ceasefire should be established "immediately throughout Sierra Leone".
Members of the junta delegation said before the talks there could be no question of Kabbah returning to power but they did not oppose an early return to constitutional legality.
They also called for Nigeria to let rebel leader Foday Sankoh return to Sierra Leone.

Corporal Tamba Gborie, who led the coup and installed Major Johnny Paul Koroma as military leader, said it would be impossible to strike a deal without Sankoh, who remains under effective house arrest in Nigeria.
Koroma has named Sankoh, who was listed on the Freetown delegation, as his number two. "You can't make any peace in Sierra Leone without Foday Sankoh," Gborie said.
Nigeria, which heads a West African force trying to restore peace and democracy to both Sierra Leone and neighbouring Liberia, has spearheaded efforts to restore Kabbah.

Ivory Coast, Nigeria, Ghana and Guinea were given the job of holding talks with the junta and reporting back to Nigeria's military ruler, General Sani Abacha, current chairman of the Economic Community of West African States.
Ikimi held separate talks with members of the junta's delegation before Friday's session, witnesses said.
Liberia holds national elections on Saturday to end seven years of civil war and officials said that Ikimi and the other foreign ministers planned to be there.
"Peace in Liberia will not be long-lasting if there is not peace in Sierra Leone," Ikimi told the meeting on Thursday.
Nigerian soldiers have clashed with Sierra Leone troops and their rebel allies on several occasions since Nigerian gunboats bombarded the capital in a June 2 show of force.
Ivory Coast brokered a peace deal last year between Kabbah and Sankoh's rebels. It did not hold. The rebels rallied to the coup, flooding into the capital Freetown for the first time.
